newsitem.title: CANADA: Toronto Exchange CEO calls for national regulator.
newsitem.headline: Toronto Exchange CEO calls for national regulator.

text.p: The Bre-X Minerals Ltd fiasco highlights the need for a national securities regulator in Canada, Toronto Stock Exchange President and Chief Executive Rowland Fleming said on Tuesday.

Investors have lost billions of dollars on Bre-X, a company once valued at C$6 billion, which sank to penny stock status on Tuesday after a report on Sunday revealed large-scale tampering with samples from its celebrated Busang property in Indonesia.
The find, once touted as the largest this century, now appears to be worthless.
Fleming said if there was anything positive to be gained from Bre-X, "it is yet another compelling argument for the long overdue formation of a national securities commission in Canada."
There are 12 securities commissions in Canada, which Fleming said compared poorly with one each in the United States, Britain, Germany and Japan among others.
"No exchange may be able to stop the next Bre-X from happening," Fleming said in a speech prepared for the Corporate Secretaries Congress.

"But I would argue that a single securities commission can certainly make that possibility much more remote -- just as it did in Australia in the wake of a nickel scandal similar to Bre-X in the 1980s -- and a single commission can react much more quickly when a scandal of this proportion occurs."
Fleming defended the TSE's role in the Bre-X scandal, saying that the company more than met the exchange's listing requirements.
Bre-X was first listed on the Alberta Stock Exchange and under current securities laws, less disclosure is required for a secondary issue than a secondary one.

"But if someone is simply lying, in a huge and stupendous fashion, as appears to be the case with Bre-X, all the disclosure rules in the world will not protect either the gullible investor or, it seems, even the most sophisticated one," Fleming said.

He said Bre-X was a mining exploration company and carried all the risks inherent with that. He said the TSE examined a substantial pre-feasibility report from a reputable company, Kilborn Engineering.
